source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Core theory. Holistic thought attends to the whole field and the relations between object and field, uses experience-based knowledge, and is dialectical (change, contradiction, Middle Way). Analytic thought detaches the object from context, assigns it to categories, and uses rules and formal logic, avoiding contradiction. The authors say the two cover both reasoning and perception.
numbers: Definitions only. No single effect size. The paper is a narrative review, mostly of student samples; the authors say they 'will not provide details about samples'.
quote: We define holistic thought as involving an orientation to the context or field as a whole
limits: Interpretive review, not a meta-analysis. Evidence is selective. The authors say North Americans may differ more from East Asians than Europeans or Latin Americans do.
agent_relevance: Gives two named framings to apply as O6/O8 alternative framings: object plus category plus rule, versus field plus relation plus context. Use as a checklist, not as a claim about the model's culture.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Causal chain proposed: social organisation (personal agency vs collective harmony) leads to what people attend to, then to metaphysics (discrete objects vs continuous field), tacit epistemology, and cognitive process. Origin is 'distally materialistic but proximally social': Chinese rice-farming cooperation and a centralised state vs Greek mountains, herding, trade and city-state debate. Stability comes from 'socio-cognitive homeostasis'.
numbers: No numbers. Supporting evidence cited: Berry and Witkin found farmers more field dependent than hunters, herders and industrial peoples; Orthodox Jewish boys more field dependent than secular Jewish boys, with IQ controlled.
limits: The authors call the origin story speculative. The ancient China-Greece contrast rests on secondary historians. Later work tests rice vs wheat directly (Talhelm line below).
agent_relevance: The theory says thinking style follows what the task makes you attend to. So a scaffold can steer the framing by what it makes salient.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Masuda and Nisbett (2000, reported here): Japanese and Americans described 20-s animated underwater scenes. Americans started with the focal fish; Japanese started with the background (lake, pond). Mentions of focal-fish details were equal across groups. In recognition, Japanese were hurt when the focal fish was shown on a wrong background; Americans were not.
numbers: Japanese made about 70 percent more statements about background and about 100 percent more statements about relations involving inanimate parts of the scene. Sample sizes not given in this review.
limits: Review gives percentages only. Exact N and tests are in the original JPSP paper (see the PubMed abstract line below).
agent_relevance: The effect is about where attention goes first and what gets bound to the object, not total detail. An agent test should compare what it mentions first and what it binds, not only how much it says.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Covariation detection (Ji, Peng, Nisbett): Chinese judged more covariation between arbitrary figure pairs than Americans, were more confident, and better calibrated. Americans showed a primacy effect when predicting future covariation; Chinese did not.
numbers: True covariation ranged from r = .00 to .60. With control (a button to choose the stimulus and the interval), Americans saw more covariation and were more confident; Chinese showed the opposite and their calibration got worse.
limits: Secondary report of in-press work. No N in the review.
agent_relevance: Holistic attention has a measurable payoff (better calibration of association) and a cost (field dependence). The narrow focus is not simply worse or better.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Rod-and-frame test (Ji et al., in press): East Asians made more errors than Americans matched on SAT math, and were less confident. With control over the rod, American males improved; the other groups did not.
numbers: Groups matched on SAT math score. No error rates or N in the review.
limits: Control effect involved gender (American males only). Cells likely small.
agent_relevance: Field dependence is the cost of holistic processing; an agent that cannot ignore a misleading context frame shows the field-dependent pattern.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Attribution. Choi and Nisbett used the Jones-Harris attitude-attribution paradigm: Koreans who had themselves written a forced-side essay inferred much weaker attitudes in the target than Koreans in the standard no-choice condition; Americans made equally strong inferences in both. Morris and Peng: Americans explained mass murders by dispositions, Chinese by situation and society. Lee et al.: Hong Kong sports editorials were more contextual than US ones. Miller (1984): Hindu Indians used more role and context explanations than Americans.
numbers: Exact means not reported in the review.
limits: Koreans were sensitive to a salient situational constraint; the effect shrinks when the situation is not salient. East Asians still make dispositional attributions in many settings.
agent_relevance: A model for a debiasing probe: restate the case with the situation made salient (O6) and check whether the explanation shifts.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Physical causation. Peng and Nisbett (2000): Chinese gave more field-based explanations ('the ball is more buoyant than the water') for ambiguous hydrodynamic, aerodynamic and magnetic events; for lever and billiard-ball events both groups explained almost identically. Morris and Peng fish cartoons: Chinese saw an individual fish's motion as caused by external factors, Americans by internal ones.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Boundary condition: the effect shows for ambiguous events and vanishes for clear mechanical ones.
agent_relevance: Framing differences matter most where the problem is under-determined. On well-specified tasks, switching framing buys little, which supports G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Hindsight and surprise (Choi and Nisbett). Good Samaritan scenario: Americans and Koreans both said about 80 percent probability that the seminarian would help. Told he did NOT help, Americans still said 80 percent and were very surprised; Koreans said about 50 percent and were little surprised. Koreans were also not more surprised by two competing theories than by one. Koreans judged fewer facts in a detective story to be irrelevant than European Americans did (Asian Americans in between).
numbers: About 80 vs about 50 percent in the no-help condition. Cell sizes not given in the review.
limits: The authors read this as a cost of holism: any outcome seems explainable, so less surprise and less curiosity. Response style or modesty norms are rival readings.
agent_relevance: A warning for O8: broad reframing can make every outcome look explained. The schema should require a prediction that could be wrong before accepting a holistic story (G3).

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Categorisation. Chiu (1972) triads with children: Chinese children grouped by relation ('the mother takes care of the baby'), American children by category ('both are adults'). Ji and Nisbett repeated it with adults tested in their own languages: Chinese chose relational or functional pairs and justified them by relation, Americans chose category pairs. Norenzayan et al.: a majority of East Asians chose the family-resemblance group, a majority of European Americans the rule group, Asian Americans split equally.
numbers: Majority splits only; no percentages in the review.
limits: Later work (Ji, Zhang, Nisbett 2004) asks whether the testing language changes this; see other angle files.
agent_relevance: The triad task is the cheapest test of framing preference for an LLM, and every LLM study below uses it.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Rules vs experience (Norenzayan et al.). Category learning with cartoon animals (Venus and Saturn): East Asians and Americans were equal at exemplar-based learning; East Asians were slower in the rule condition and made more errors when rule and similarity conflicted. Typicality: Koreans found typical conclusions (eagles) more convincing than atypical ones (penguins) for logically identical arguments; European Americans did not; the gap vanished when typicality was made salient. Belief bias: Koreans more often called valid syllogisms invalid when the conclusion was implausible, yet both groups were equal on abstract items.
numbers: Equal accuracy on abstract items shows equal logical ability. No other numbers in the review.
limits: Differences shrink when the relevant feature is made salient, so these are habits (defaults), not ability limits.
agent_relevance: Key for scaffold design: the difference is a default, not a capability. A prompt can flip a default, so the agent can use both modes if told which to apply.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Dialectics (Peng and Nisbett 1999). Chinese gave 'Middle Way' answers to mother-daughter conflicts; Americans picked a side. Natural-science graduate students: Americans preferred the non-contradiction (first cause) argument for God, Chinese preferred the holism argument. With two contradictory studies, Americans rated the more plausible one MORE plausible than when it was seen alone (polarising); Chinese rated the two as equal and raised the weaker one. Davis et al.: adding weak anti-arguments made Koreans less favourable to funding and Americans more favourable. Briley et al.: asked to justify a choice, Americans moved to an extreme option, East Asians to the compromise.
numbers: Before justification, Americans and East Asians were about equally likely to pick the middle option of a triad.
limits: The authors note that the analytic stance gives no guarantee against bad inference: weak counter-arguments made Americans MORE confident. Both responses are normatively questionable.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G4 and G5: hardening on a weak counter-argument (analytic) and splitting the difference (holistic) are both errors. A critic should score argument strength, not take a side.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108, 291-310
finding: Other attention results. Chinese Americans gave more whole-card Rorschach responses than European Americans (Abel and Hsu 1949). Park, Nisbett and Hedden: Chinese but not Americans recalled words better when they were printed on a social background card.
numbers: Counts not given in the review.
limits: Rorschach study used Chinese Americans, not Chinese, and is from 1949. The recall study is in-press work.
agent_relevance: Context as a retrieval cue is a real mechanism for holistic recall; a scaffold that stores the situation with each fact may gain the same benefit.

source: Nisbett and Masuda (2003) Culture and point of view. PNAS 100, 11163-11170
finding: Updated statement of the theory with the environment added. Miyamoto and Nisbett photographed post offices, schools and hotels in New York and Tokyo, Ann Arbor and Hikone, and Chelsea and Torahime. Japanese scenes held more objects and vaguer boundaries.
numbers: Japanese scenes had 32 percent more objects (edge counts with NIH Image) than American scenes, at every town size. Students of both nations rated Japanese scenes as having more objects and more ambiguous boundaries.
limits: Photo sampling of three building types, one town pair per size.
agent_relevance: The environment affords the style: the same person attends differently to object-salient and field-salient scenes. So the context given to the agent can shape the framing it uses.

source: Nisbett and Masuda (2003) Culture and point of view. PNAS 100, 11163-11170
finding: Fish scenes (Masuda and Nisbett): after seeing each 20-s video twice, Americans began their report with salient objects far more often; Japanese began with the field almost twice as often as Americans. Recognition of 45 old and 45 new objects shown on original, no, or novel background: American accuracy was unaffected; Japanese made substantially more errors on the novel background.
numbers: Japanese made 65 percent more observations about the field and nearly twice as many object-field relations. Ten vignettes. Japanese were better with no background than a novel one, but not worse than with the original.
limits: This review says 65 percent where the 2001 review says 70 percent for background statements; treat 65 to 70 as the range.
agent_relevance: A clean, repeatable measurement: first-mention order plus recognition under background swap. It can be run on a vision-language model.

source: Nisbett and Masuda (2003) Culture and point of view. PNAS 100, 11163-11170
finding: Change blindness (Masuda and Nisbett): Americans detected more changes in salient focal objects; Japanese detected more changes in relations and background. Both nations found object changes easier in American-style scenes and field changes easier in Japanese-style scenes.
numbers: Counts shown only in figures.
limits: The scene-type effect in both groups means part of the difference is the stimuli people meet.
agent_relevance: Salience in the input steers the framing for everyone; reordering or reformatting a problem is a cheap way to move an agent's focus (O6).

source: Nisbett and Masuda (2003) Culture and point of view. PNAS 100, 11163-11170
finding: Art and drawing. East Asian students drew landscapes with a higher horizon and more objects than Americans. Japanese portrait photos showed the person small relative to the field; Americans often took close-ups. Ji et al.: when asked whether a described state (for example a romance) would continue or change, Chinese expected more change.
numbers: Descriptive; Japanese participants 'literally never' made portraits with the person as large a share of the frame as the American close-up.
limits: No inferential statistics in the review.
agent_relevance: The landscape-drawing task (object count and horizon height) is the one applied to image generators in Hu et al. (2026).

source: Chua, Boland, Nisbett (2005) Cultural variation in eye movements during scene perception. PNAS 102, 12629-12633
finding: Eye tracking: Americans fixated the focal object sooner and looked at it longer; Chinese made more fixations, all of the extra on the background.
numbers: 25 European American and 27 Chinese graduate students recruited; 21 and 24 analysed. 36 scenes, 3 s each. Americans reached the object 118 ms sooner, t(43)=2.41, p=.02. Chinese made more fixations overall, F(1,43)=4.43, p<.05, entirely on the background, F(1,43)=9.50, p<.005. Time course: Americans favoured the object 420-1100 ms, Chinese the background 1100-3000 ms.
limits: Small, graduate-student sample. Fixation counts are in figures only. Read through a page summary, so test details are limited to what it gave. Other angle files cover later replication doubts.
agent_relevance: The difference is in attention timing, not in what is seen at all. It maps to the design choice of where the first step of a scaffold goes.

source: Chua, Boland, Nisbett (2005) Cultural variation in eye movements during scene perception. PNAS 102, 12629-12633
finding: East Asians were less accurate at recognising objects on new backgrounds. This is a conceptual replication of the Masuda-Nisbett recognition result, with eye movements added.
numbers: F(1,44)=5.72, p=.02. Chinese liked the pictures more than Americans did (4.64 vs 4.16, p<.005).
limits: Same sample limits as the line above.
agent_relevance: Binding of object to context is a reproduced result, so a background-swap test is a good probe for context binding in a vision-language model.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33, 61-83
finding: Challenges the East-West framing. Analytic-holistic differences also appear in Arabs, Malaysians, Russians, Turkish herders vs farmers, and subsistence farmers (Mapuche in Chile, Sangu in Tanzania). So the split may be West vs most everyone else, with Westerners at the extreme. European Americans are the outlier in rule vs family-resemblance categorisation, compared with East Asians and Turkish Black Sea communities.
numbers: Rod-and-frame: Canadians less field dependent than Chinese, who were less field dependent than Arabs. Mapuche and Sangu classification resembled the Chinese pattern but exaggerated toward holistic. Only Westerners and migratory foragers sit consistently at the field-independent end (Witkin and Berry 1975).
quote: Westerners are not unique in their cognitive styles, but they do occupy the extreme end of the distribution
limits: A review that compiles studies from many sources. The East-West contrast is not the full picture.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'Western analytic, Eastern holistic' as two modes of a model. The analytic mode may be the unusual one, which fits LLMs trained on WEIRD text being analytic on some tests.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world?
finding: Self-construal as a cause: independent self-construal primes raise analytic processing and interdependent primes raise holistic processing (Oyserman and Lee 2008). Regional contrasts inside countries run the same way: Northern vs Southern Italians, Hokkaido vs mainland Japanese, Western vs Eastern Europeans (Varnum et al. 2008).
numbers: No effect sizes in the review.
limits: These are the review's claims. Priming effects have faced replication doubts and are not checked in this file.
agent_relevance: If framing can be primed in humans, a self-construal-like prompt cue may be a cheap way to shift an LLM's framing. Treat it as a hypothesis to test.

source: Talhelm et al. (2014) Large-scale psychological differences within China explained by rice versus wheat agriculture. Science 344, 603-608
finding: Within one country, Han Chinese from rice-growing southern regions were more interdependent and holistic than those from wheat-growing northern regions. The effect held in neighbouring counties along the rice-wheat border, which argues against a climate explanation. Modernisation and pathogen theories did not fit.
numbers: 1162 Han Chinese participants at six sites.
limits: Only the PubMed abstract page was read. The study is correlational. A response by Ruan and Xie (IFPRI 2014) questions the rice-individualism link; not opened by this angle.
agent_relevance: A within-nation test of the theory: the divide follows work practice, not race or language. This supports reading style as a habit shaped by task structure.

source: Masuda and Nisbett (2001) Attending holistically versus analytically: comparing the context sensitivity of Japanese and Americans. JPSP 81, 922-934
finding: Study 1: Japanese and Americans watched animated underwater scenes and reported what they saw, then did a recognition test with original and novel settings. Study 2 repeated recognition with wildlife photographs. Japanese made more statements about context and relationships and recognised objects better in their original setting; setting changes had little effect on Americans.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract page; percentages are in the Nisbett reviews above.
limits: Abstract page only; full paper not read.
agent_relevance: The canonical attention-to-context experiment, and the template for vision-language tests.

source: Rhode, Voyer, Gleibs (2016) Does language matter? Exploring Chinese-Korean differences in holistic perception. Frontiers in Psychology 7:1508
finding: Conceptual replication of Tajima and Duffield (2012): picture description by English, Chinese and Korean speakers. Koreans mentioned the most ground information, Chinese next, English fewest. Recall of ground information did not differ.
numbers: N=90 in total. Mean ground items in description: Korean 10.97 (SD 3.38), Chinese 7.70 (2.12), English 5.10 (1.88); F(2,87)=39.99, p<.001, eta-squared .48. d = -2.15 Korean vs English, -1.30 English vs Chinese, -1.16 Korean vs Chinese. Recall: F(2,87)=0.997, p=.37.
limits: Description differed but recall did not, so the effect may be 'thinking for speaking' not perception. The authors say it challenges a pan-Asian holistic bias.
agent_relevance: Output-language structure can change how much context a description carries without changing what was seen. The same warning applies to LLM outputs.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu, Cui (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker?
finding: First LLM test using the Analysis-Holism Scale (AHS, 24 items: attention, causality, change, contradiction) and the Triadic Categorization Task (TCT). GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 scored holistic against human norms on the AHS and had a high relational share on the TCT. On value scales (DSS, SCS) they did not clearly lean East or West.
numbers: AHS (7-point): GPT-3.5 M=5.35 (SD .11, 10 runs), GPT-4 M=5.01 (SD .10), human norm 4.87 (SD .49, N=702), both p<.001. TCT relational share: GPT-3.5 0.87, GPT-4 0.85, above most Chinese provinces. DSS: GPT-3.5 4.59 vs 4.00 (p<.001); GPT-4 3.97 (p=.344). SCS-independent 6.98 and 5.32 vs 4.73; SCS-interdependent 5.85 and 4.95 vs 4.81 (GPT-4 p=.07).
limits: Only 10 runs per model at temperature 1. Tiny SDs make t-tests against human norms overstate certainty. Stated to be robust to temperature and prompt language. GPT-3.5 near-ceiling 'strongly agree' (SCS-Ind 6.98 of 7) suggests acquiescence.
agent_relevance: LLMs lean to the holistic end on a triad test. But Atari et al. (below) found the opposite on a different triad set, so the result depends on items and prompt.

source: Jin et al. (2023)
finding: Authors explain the holistic result by training: next-token prediction uses the whole context and finds global patterns rather than strict logical analysis; RLHF may steer style. They note English-heavy training could predict an analytic style, yet the result was holistic.
numbers: Argument only. No ablation of training data or RLHF.
limits: Two competing hypotheses are given and not separated by any experiment.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a model's default is analytic. Measure the default on a few triad and attribution probes before choosing which framing O6 adds.

source: Atari, Xue, Park, Blasi, Henrich (2023) Which Humans? (preprint)
finding: GPT's survey answers match WEIRD populations most. On the triad task GPT looked most like people from the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden and Ireland, i.e. analytic, the opposite of Jin et al.'s holistic reading.
numbers: GPT queried 1,100 times with 20 triads. Correlation of GPT-human similarity with WEIRDness distance from the US: r = -.70 (49 nations), Spearman -.72, multilevel B = -0.90 (SE .16). Human triad data: 31 populations from yourmorals.org. Similarity also correlated .85 with HDI, .85 with log GDP, and .69 with Internet use.
limits: Triad items and prompt wording differ from Jin et al. Comparison is with online samples. Preprint. The r = -.70 is for all survey variables, not the triad task alone.
agent_relevance: The two studies disagree, so read which items were used before drawing a rule. For an agent: the default framing depends on items; do not infer a trait from one test.

source: Sabir, Gasper, Loem, Sharma (2025) Contrasting cognitive styles in vision-language models: holistic attention in Japanese versus analytical focus in English
finding: Captioned COCO images with English and Japanese VLMs; GPT-4o judged whether each caption began with background (holistic) or object (analytic). Most captions were analytic in all models; Japanese-prompted models were somewhat more holistic, and Japanese-culture images raised the holistic share.
numbers: 5K filtered COCO images, 5-shot: GPT-4o 19.22 percent holistic; GPT-4o-JP 23.64; Gemma-3-12B 14.16; VILA-JP-14B 13.88. GPT-4o-JP balanced 6-shot 28.64. On 1K Japanese photos GPT-4o-JP balanced reached 73.37 percent holistic (about 47 points above COCO). Human check of 200 captions by three Japanese speakers: GPT-4o-JP 17.75 percent holistic, VILA-JP 15.33.
limits: The classifier is GPT-4o with few-shot prompts and the holistic share moves with the prompt (23.64 vs 28.64 for the same model). The human check gave lower rates (17.75) than GPT-4o rating the same model (29.00). Only English and Japanese. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A VLM changes its framing with output language and image content. What is put in front of the model is a stronger lever than its 'cultural identity'.

source: Sabir et al. (2025)
finding: Translation test: human English COCO captions vs human Japanese captions (Yahoo-COCO), plus machine translation each way. Holistic share moved about 13 points with translation and recovered about 10 points on back-translation. The Japanese-trained VILA-JP was less holistic than GPT-4o-JP, so language alone does not set the style.
numbers: Eng-original 12.34 percent holistic, JP machine-translated 27.54, Eng back-translated 15.20, JP-original 27.48, ENG machine-translated 16.26, JP back-translated 26.58. Random 1K images: GPT4o-JP 35.50 percent holistic vs VILA-JP-14B 24.00.
limits: The 'mentioned first' measure may be driven by Japanese word order and syntax. Similar confound to Rhode et al. (2016).
agent_relevance: Use a content measure (number of relations used), not only first-mention order, when testing an agent for holistic framing.

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung, Peng (2026) Beyond instrumental and substitutive paradigms: Machine Culture in large language models
finding: Crossed a Chinese model (ERNIE 4.5 / iRAG-1.0) with a US model (GPT-4o / DALL-E 3) and Chinese vs English prompts on eight tasks; four were holistic-analytic (landscape drawing, scene description, attribution, triad). Model origin did not predict the human-like direction: the US model was often MORE holistic. Prompt language did not reliably switch styles.
numbers: 100 iterations per condition, temperature 1. Landscape object count: US model 11.53 (SD 4.39), more than the Chinese model; horizon height US 533.47 vs Chinese 519.79 (d=0.34). Scene description objects: Chinese model 12.31 (SD 1.63) vs US 8.66 (1.37), d=2.42. Triad relational-minus-categorical score: US 8.10 (SD 1.44) vs Chinese 6.04 (1.54), d=1.38, opposite to the human East Asian pattern.
limits: One model per origin. Results inconsistent across tasks. One author is a founder of the field (Kaiping Peng). Preprint; evaluator models score some tasks.
agent_relevance: If the same model gives opposite answers on drawing and on text, the style is task-bound. A scaffold must test the framing on the task at hand and not rely on a model-level trait.

source: Hu et al. (2026)
finding: Prompt-language effect ('cultural reversal'): Chinese prompts raised object count in landscape generation (10.71 vs 8.91, d=0.49) but did not change horizon height; in scene description English prompts gave more objects than Chinese (10.90 vs 10.06). On the triad task the Chinese model scored lower on relational thinking in Chinese (5.30) than in English (6.78). Attribution was asymmetric: the Chinese model moved toward individual attribution in English; the US model did not respond to language.
limits: The authors suggest English text density explains verbose English output. Cross-language comparisons confound language with verbosity.
agent_relevance: Switching the prompt language is not a dependable way to switch an LLM's framing. Use explicit, task-level framing instructions (O6) and measure the effect.

source: Choi, Koo, Choi (2007) An Analysis-Holism Scale. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
finding: A 24-item Analysis-Holism Scale with four factors (attention, causality, change, contradiction), validated over six studies. Used by Jin et al. 2023 for ChatGPT. Seen only through a search summary.
numbers: 24 items; six studies; no reliability figures confirmed.
limits: Not opened. Self-report scale; scores may reflect response style.
agent_relevance: AHS items are a cheap four-part probe of an LLM's stated framing, but self-report on an LLM measures its stated stance, not its behaviour.
